report.markdown:
## Training Plan: 14-month rescue border collie mix (leash pulling + dog-directed barking)

### 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?
**Hire a trainer for a short, focused engagement** — you don't need an ongoing weekly commitment, just 3-5 private sessions to get a correct evaluation and protocol, then run the daily repetition yourself.

Why:
- Border collies are high-drive/high-arousal; reacting to *every* dog on walks is true leash reactivity, not just excitement, and getting the counter-conditioning approach right early prevents it from becoming a rehearsed habit.
- Unknown history (rescue) means a trainer can rule out fear vs. frustration vs. under-socialization as the driver — that changes the protocol.
- Avoid e-collar/correction-based trainers as a first choice for this profile; stick to reward-based, force-free trainers.

### 2. Local South Bay options with real prices

| Trainer | Location | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **South Bay Dog Training** | 186 E Sunnyoaks Ave Ste C, Campbell — (408) 673-0611 | Group reactive-dog class: **$165/3 wks** or **$220/4 wks**; private sessions also offered (price not published — ask when calling) | Reward-based; dedicated Reactive Dog Level 1–3 class; open evenings & Saturdays |
| **D For Dogz (Kaajal "KT")** | Serves San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Campbell, Los Gatos, Palo Alto, etc. — 650-538-3011 | Not published online; free intro call, then private session pricing by quote | Specializes specifically in leash-reactive dogs; positive reinforcement; open Mon-Fri 9-7, Sun 9-3 (evening slots available) |
| **Blue Leash Dog Training** | Bay Area | Private lessons from **$175/hr**, package discounts available | Free 15-min phone consult; runs dedicated leash-reactivity workshops |

*Skipped:* Off Leash K9 Training (San Jose/SF) — e-collar-based, $500 first lesson + $100/session — not recommended as a first approach for a rescue with reactivity and unknown history.

**Recommended next step:** call South Bay Dog Training and D For Dogz, ask for an evaluation/first private session, evening or weekend slot.

### 3. Week-by-week plan (first 4 weeks)

**Week 1 — Foundations, no dog exposure pressure**
- 2x daily 5–10 min sessions: hand-target, name/check-in, sit, reward marker word.
- Switch to a front-clip harness or head halter to cut pulling leverage immediately.
- Walk quiet routes/times, keep distance from other dogs — goal is zero reactive outbursts, not proximity.
- Book the trainer eval for early Week 2.

**Week 2 — Loose-leash walking + trainer evaluation**
- Trainer session happens this week; get a customized protocol and adjust plan as needed.
- Practice loose-leash walking in low-distraction areas (yard, driveway, quiet street).
- Start the "engage-disengage" game: mark/reward the dog noticing another dog at a distance it can stay calm at.

**Week 3 — Distance work around triggers**
- Structured "dog neutrality" walks in open areas (parking lots, park edges) where other dogs are visible at a safe distance.
- High-value treats reserved only for these sessions.
- Decrease distance only as long as the dog stays calm/quiet; if barking starts, add distance — don't punish.
- One dedicated 20–30 min weekend "reactive dog walk."

**Week 4 — Generalize and add duration**
- Practice on 2–3 different routes/neighborhoods.
- Layer in duration/distraction: near a stationary dog, then a slow-moving dog, before closer passes.
- Reassess with the trainer — reactivity work is typically a months-long process; treat week 4 as a checkpoint, not a finish line.

**Throughout:** avoid letting the dog rehearse the reactive behavior when possible (cross the street, U-turn); reward calm behavior heavily; keep sessions short, end on success; no corrections/punishment for barking — it tends to worsen fear-based reactivity.

subtasks.title: Decide DIY vs hiring a trainer
subtasks.description:
Recommendation: Hire a trainer, at least for a short focused engagement, rather than going fully DIY.

Reasoning:
- Border collies are high-drive, high-arousal dogs; barking/lunging at every dog is true leash reactivity, not just excitement, and poor early handling can entrench it.
- A 14-month rescue is still in an impressionable window — getting the counter-conditioning protocol right early is much easier than fixing a rehearsed reactive habit later.
- You don't need a large commitment: 3-5 private sessions (or one evaluation + a handful of follow-ups) from a reward-based trainer to get an assessment and a correct protocol, then you can run most of the day-to-day repetition yourself on evenings/weekends.
- Avoid e-collar/correction-based programs for reactivity in an unknown-history rescue dog — reputable reward-based trainers are the safer starting point for a rescue with unknown history.

Best fit if you want a structured reactive-dog class alongside private work.

3. Blue Leash Dog Training — one-on-one custom lessons starting at $175/hr with discount packages available; runs focused reactivity workshops and free pack walks. Offers a free 15-min phone consult to start.

subtasks.title: Draft week-by-week 4-week training plan
subtasks.description:
Week 1: Foundations at home, zero dog exposure pressure.
- Daily 5-10 min sessions (2x/day): hand-target, name-recognition/check-in, "sit," reward-marker word ("yes!").
- Switch to front-clip harness or head halter (e.g. Freedom Harness/Gentle Leader) for walks to reduce pulling leverage immediately.
- Walks: choose quiet routes/times, keep distance from other dogs (across the street or farther) — the goal this week is zero reactive outbursts, not proximity.
- Book the trainer evaluation session for early Week 2 (see hiring subtask).

Week 2: Loose-leash walking + trainer evaluation.
- Trainer eval/first session happens this week — get a customized reactivity protocol from them and confirm/adjust the plan below.
- Practice loose-leash walking in the yard/driveway/quiet street using stop-and-reward or 300 Peck-style pattern games.
- Introduce "engage-disengage" game: mark and reward whenever dog notices another dog at a distance it can stay calm at, before any reaction.
- Continue daily short obedience reps (sit/down/stay/come).

Week 3: Distance work around triggers.
- Begin structured "dog neutrality" walks: find open areas (parking lots, park edges) where other dogs are visible at a distance the dog can stay under threshold.
- Use high-value treats (chicken, cheese) reserved only for these sessions.
- Gradually decrease distance to other dogs only as long as dog stays calm/quiet — if barking starts, you're too close; add distance, don't punish.
- Weekend: one dedicated 20-30 min "reactive dog walk" in a location good for this (per trainer's suggestion).

Week 4: Generalize and add duration.
- Practice on 2-3 different routes/neighborhoods so skills aren't location-specific.
- Start layering in duration/distraction: walking near a stationary dog, then a slow-moving dog, before attempting closer passes.
- Reassess with trainer: are you ready to reduce distance further, or do you need another few weeks at this stage? Reactivity work is rarely "done" in 4 weeks — expect this to be an ongoing, months-long process with the 4-week point being a re-evaluation checkpoint, not a finish line.

General rules throughout: never let the dog rehearse the reactive behavior if avoidable (cross the street, U-turn); reward calm behavior heavily; keep sessions short and end on success; avoid corrections/punishment for barking as it typically worsens fear-based reactivity.
